Absorption of Fermionic Dark Matter via the Scalar Portal

Peter Cox Email: peter.cox@unimelb.edu.au Affiliation: ARC Centre of Excellence for Dark Matter Particle Physics,
School of Physics, The University of Melbourne, Victoria 3010, Australia    Matthew J. Dolan Email: matthew.dolan@unimelb.edu.au Affiliation: ARC Centre of Excellence for Dark Matter Particle Physics,
School of Physics, The University of Melbourne, Victoria 3010, Australia    Joshua Wood Email: jwood5@student.unimelb.edu.au Affiliation: ARC Centre of Excellence for Dark Matter Particle Physics,
School of Physics, The University of Melbourne, Victoria 3010, Australia
Abstract

The absorption of fermionic dark matter has recently been studied as a signature for the direct detection of dark matter. We construct the first UV completion of the scalar effective operator associated with this signature. We calculate the constraints on the model and demonstrate there is viable parameter space which can be probed by a next-generation experiment such as XLZD. We also consider the cosmological history of our model and show that the correct relic abundance can be obtained via freeze-out in the dark sector. However, within this minimal model, we find that the absorption signal is highly suppressed in the parameter space that yields the correct relic abundance.

I Introduction

The direct detection of dark matter in terrestrial experiments remains one of the most promising strategies for understanding its microscopic properties. The traditional approach to direct detection involves searching for the elastic scattering of dark matter on nuclei (χ​N→χ​N)(\chi N\to\chi N), and has produced strong bounds on dark matter–nucleon interactions for dark matter masses in the GeV – TeV range [1]. However, within the landscape of dark matter models there are a range of potential direct detection signals beyond elastic nuclear (or electron) scattering. An interesting class of signals arise from inelastic processes in which the dark matter is absorbed.

Dark matter absorption processes are, of course, used extensively to search for light bosonic dark matter, for example axions and dark photons. On the other hand, the direct detection of fermionic dark matter through absorption has been comparatively less explored. This is despite the fact that it occurs generically in models where there is no stabilising symmetry for the dark matter. The requirement that dark matter is long-lived on cosmological timescales leads to strongly suppressed interactions unless the dark matter is sufficiently light. Hence, fermionic dark matter can yield an observable absorption signal only for keV-scale masses, once the lower bound of mχ≳m_{\chi}\gtrsim keV [2, 3] from Pauli exclusion is also taken into account. While keV-scale dark matter is challenging to detect in elastic scattering experiments, absorption processes have the advantage that the entire rest mass energy of the dark matter can be deposited in the detector.

In this paper, we focus on fermionic dark matter absorption via interaction with electrons11 1 Fermionic dark matter absorption via interaction with nucleons has been considered in [4, 5, 6]., specifically the process e​χ→e​νe\chi\to e\nu. This process was first considered in the context of sterile neutrino dark matter via active-sterile mixing [4]; however, in that scenario the potentially accessible parameter space is excluded by X-ray constraints on decaying dark matter [7]. More recently, it was revisited in Refs. [8, 9], which used an effective field theory (EFT) approach to investigate the sensitivity of existing and future experiments. The PandaX-4T experiment has subsequently performed a dedicated search for this signal [10].

An advantage of the EFT approach is its model-independence; however, one must also consider whether or not there exist viable ultraviolet (UV) completions. There are several additional, non-trivial requirements that the UV completion must satisfy: cosmological stability of dark matter and observational bounds on its decay; constraints on the mediator from both terrestrial experiments and astrophysics; a viable dark matter production mechanism and thermal history; and invariance under the full Standard Model (SM) gauge group. As we shall demonstrate, the combination of these considerations can be highly constraining, and may exclude the possibility of observing a signal in future direct detection experiments.

In this work, we present a minimal UV completion of the scalar22 2 For a UV completion of the vector operator (χ¯​γμ​PR​ν)​(e¯​γμ​e)(\bar{\chi}\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}\nu)(\bar{e}\gamma^{\mu}e) see [8]. That paper also proposed a scalar-mediated simplified model, but this requires a UV completion to be invariant under the SM gauge group. operator (χ¯​PR​ν)​(e¯​e)(\bar{\chi}P_{R}\nu)(\bar{e}e). In addition to the Dirac fermion dark matter χ\chi, the model features a right-handed sterile neutrino and a scalar mediator that mixes with the Higgs, leading to the absorption process shown in fig. 1. The sterile neutrino is simultaneously responsible for generating Dirac neutrino mass.

There are several complementary probes of our model, some of which already provide strong bounds on the parameter space. First, the decay χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma is tightly constrained by X-ray observations for dark matter masses above 15 keV. There are also strong bounds on the scalar mediator from horizontal branch stars and supernova 1987A. Taking these constraints into account, we show that there remains parameter space that could be probed by a next-generation liquid xenon direct detection experiment, if one ignores the additional requirement of a viable dark matter production mechanism.

In much of the parameter space, including the region of potential interest for direct detection, the dark sector self-thermalises and the relic abundance is produced by freeze-out in the dark sector. We show that this mechanism can yield the observed relic abundance, but simultaneously predicts a highly suppressed direct detection signal. Contrary to the naïve expectations of the EFT analysis, we conclude that in a minimal UV completion direct detection is not a powerful probe of the model.

The structure of the paper is as follows. In section II we present our UV completion of the scalar operator. Section III discusses the phenomenology of the model, including dark matter decays, and collider and astrophysical bounds on the scalar mediator. Production of the dark matter is addressed in section IV, before we conclude in section V.

II The Model

We begin by introducing a UV complete model that can, in principle, yield an observable direct detection signal. At the level of the EFT, the scalar-mediated dark matter absorption process e​χ→e​νe\chi\to e\nu proceeds via the dimension-6 operator/s

1Λ2​(χ¯​PL,R​ν)​(e¯​e),\frac{1}{\Lambda^{2}}(\bar{\chi}P_{L,R}\nu)(\bar{e}e)\,, (1)

where Λ\Lambda is a scale associated with the UV completion of the effective operator. The tree-level completion of this operator is shown in fig. 1, with Λ\Lambda given in terms of UV parameters by

1Λ4=|Ye​e​Yχ​ν|2mϕ4,\frac{1}{\Lambda^{4}}=\frac{\left|Y_{ee}Y_{\chi\nu}\right|^{2}}{m_{\phi}^{4}}\,, (2)

where Ye​eY_{ee} and Yχ​νY_{\chi\nu} are the vertex factors depicted in the diagram.

The minimal UV completion features the SM Higgs as the scalar mediator and introduces a coupling to dark matter of the form yH​χ​L¯​H~​χy_{H\chi}\bar{L}\tilde{H}\chi. However, this scenario cannot yield an observable signal in direct detection. First, assuming that yH​χ∼𝒪⁡(1)y_{H\chi}\sim\mathcal{O}(1), the effective operator scale is set by the electroweak scale, combined with the electron Yukawa coupling: Λ∼mh/ye\Lambda\sim m_{h}/\sqrt{y_{e}}. This is already beyond the foreseeable reach of direct detection experiments [8]. Second, after electroweak symmetry breaking, the coupling yH​χy_{H\chi} leads to mixing between the dark matter and the active neutrinos. This enables the radiative decay χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma to proceed via a WW boson/charged lepton loop. This dark matter decay mode is highly constrained by X-ray line searches, translating into an upper bound on the coupling of yH​χ≲10−26y_{H\chi}\lesssim 10^{-26} for keV scale dark matter [11].

With the minimal scenario ruled out, we consider a new light scalar mediator. We introduce a real gauge singlet scalar field ϕ\phi that couples to the SM fermions via mixing with the Higgs. We also introduce a chiral, gauge singlet fermion νR\nu_{R} that couples to the dark matter via a term ϕ​ν¯R​χ\phi\bar{\nu}_{R}\chi. As its name suggests, νR\nu_{R} is also responsible for the generation of neutrino mass. After integrating out ϕ\phi, this model generates the operator (χ¯​PR​ν)​(e¯​e)(\bar{\chi}P_{R}\nu)(\bar{e}e).

The Lagrangian describing the model is

ℒ=ℒS​M+ℒχ+ℒνR+ℒϕ+ℒi​n​t,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{SM}+\mathcal{L}_{\chi}+\mathcal{L}_{\nu_{R}}+\mathcal{L}_{\phi}+\mathcal{L}_{int}\,, (3)

with

ℒχ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\chi} =iχ¯L′∂̸χL′+iχ¯R′∂̸χR′−Mχ(χ¯L′χR′+h.c.),\displaystyle=i\bar{\chi}^{\prime}_{L}\not{\partial}\chi^{\prime}_{L}+i\bar{\chi}^{\prime}_{R}\not{\partial}\chi^{\prime}_{R}-M_{\chi}(\bar{\chi}^{\prime}_{L}\chi^{\prime}_{R}+h.c.)\,, (4)
ℒνR\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\nu_{R}} =iν¯R′∂̸νR′−(yH​νL¯H~νR′+h.c.),\displaystyle=i\bar{\nu}^{\prime}_{R}\not{\partial}\nu^{\prime}_{R}-\big(y_{H\nu}\bar{L}\tilde{H}\nu^{\prime}_{R}+h.c.\big)\,, (5)
ℒϕ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\phi} =12​∂μϕ′​∂μϕ′−κ1​ϕ′−κ22​ϕ′2−κ33!​ϕ′3−κ44!​ϕ′4,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\mu}\phi^{\prime}\partial^{\mu}\phi^{\prime}-\kappa_{1}\phi^{\prime}-\frac{\kappa_{2}}{2}\phi^{\prime 2}-\frac{\kappa_{3}}{3!}\phi^{\prime 3}-\frac{\kappa_{4}}{4!}\phi^{\prime 4}\,, (6)
ℒi​n​t=−δ1​H†​H​ϕ′−δ22​H†​H​ϕ′2−(yϕ​χ​νϕ′χ¯′Lν′R+h.c.)−(Mχ​νχ¯′Lν′R+h.c.),\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{int}&=-\delta_{1}H^{\dagger}H\phi^{\prime}-\frac{\delta_{2}}{2}H^{\dagger}H\phi^{\prime 2}\\ &-\left(y_{\phi\chi\nu}\phi^{\prime}\bar{\chi}^{\prime}_{L}\nu^{\prime}_{R}+h.c.\right)-\left(M_{\chi\nu}\bar{\chi}^{\prime}_{L}\nu^{\prime}_{R}+h.c.\right)\,,\end{split} (7)

where we use ′ to denote fields prior to diagonalisation to the mass basis, and H~=i​σ2​H∗\tilde{H}=i\sigma^{2}H^{*}. All couplings and masses are taken to be real without loss of generality.

The above Lagrangian exhibits a U⁡(1)U(1) lepton number symmetry, with the charges of the non-SM fields given by L⁡(νR′)=L⁡(χL,R′)=+1L(\nu^{\prime}_{R})=L(\chi^{\prime}_{L,R})=+1. This has been imposed to forbid a Majorana mass term for νR\nu_{R}. For Majorana neutrinos, the dark matter absorption process in fig. 1 would be suppressed by a small active-sterile mixing angle, since the outgoing neutrino state is required to be approximately massless. This symmetry also enforces χ′\chi^{\prime} to be a Dirac fermion.

Another important feature of the Lagrangian is the absence of a L¯​H~​χ′\bar{L}\tilde{H}\chi^{\prime} coupling, which is enforced by a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry under which χ′\chi^{\prime} and ϕ′\phi^{\prime} are odd, while all other fields are even. This ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} is softly broken by κ1\kappa_{1}, κ3\kappa_{3}, δ1\delta_{1}, and Mχ​νM_{\chi\nu}, allowing ϕ′\phi^{\prime} to mix with the Higgs and for the (χ¯​PR​ν)​(e¯​e)(\bar{\chi}P_{R}\nu)(\bar{e}e) operator to be generated33 3 This can also be achieved through only spontaneous breaking of the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry by ⟨ϕ′⟩\langle\phi^{\prime}\rangle; this is a special case of the more general model., while still providing a natural suppression of the decay χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma (as discussed in Section III).

Finally, for simplicity, we consider only a single neutrino generation, which for concreteness we take to be the electron neutrino. The generalisation to three generations is relatively straightforward and is not expected to significantly affect the phenomenology of the model, but would enhance the direct detection signal by a factor of three.

II.1 Diagonalisation and Mixing

After electroweak symmetry breaking, we expand HH around its vacuum expectation value (VEV) using the usual parameterisation

H≡12​(0v+h′),H\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ v+h^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}\,, (8)

where v≈246v\approx 246 GeV and h′h^{\prime} is a real scalar field. We also re-express ϕ′\phi^{\prime} as an expansion around its VEV (which may be zero): ϕ′→ϕ′+⟨ϕ′⟩\phi^{\prime}\to\phi^{\prime}+\left<\phi^{\prime}\right>. Explicit expressions for the scalar VEVs and the resulting mass matrices in terms of the Lagrangian parameters are given in appendix A.

If either δ1\delta_{1} or δ2​⟨ϕ′⟩\delta_{2}\left<\phi^{\prime}\right> are non-zero, mixing occurs between the SM Higgs boson h′h^{\prime} and ϕ′\phi^{\prime}. The mixing can be expressed in terms of an angle θϕ\theta_{\phi}, such that

(hϕ)=(cos⁡θϕ−sin⁡θϕsin⁡θϕcos⁡θϕ)​(h′ϕ′),\begin{pmatrix}h\\ \phi\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta_{\phi}&-\sin\theta_{\phi}\\ \sin\theta_{\phi}&\cos\theta_{\phi}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}h^{\prime}\\ \phi^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}\,, (9)

where hh and ϕ\phi (unprimed) denote the heavier and lighter mass eigenstates respectively. We take mh≈125m_{h}\approx 125 GeV and ϕ\phi is the light mediator relevant for dark matter absorption.

Mixing occurs between the dark matter and neutrino via the Mχ​νM_{\chi\nu} and yϕ​χ​ν​⟨ϕ′⟩y_{\phi\chi\nu}\left<\phi^{\prime}\right> terms in the Lagrangian. The diagonalisation of the corresponding mass matrix is detailed in appendix A. The mass eigenstates (again unprimed) can be expressed in terms of real rotations:

(νL,RχL,R)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\nu_{L,R}\\ \chi_{L,R}\end{pmatrix} =(cos⁡θL,R−sin⁡θL,Rsin⁡θL,Rcos⁡θL,R)​(νL,R′χL,R′).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta_{L,R}&-\sin\theta_{L,R}\\ \sin\theta_{L,R}&\cos\theta_{L,R}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\nu^{\prime}_{L,R}\\ \chi^{\prime}_{L,R}\end{pmatrix}\,. (10)

In the massless neutrino limit, sin⁡θL\sin\theta_{L} vanishes and mixing only occurs between χR′\chi_{R}^{\prime} and νR′\nu_{R}^{\prime}. After diagonalisation, and working in this limit, the tree-level couplings between χL,R\chi_{L,R} and νL,R\nu_{L,R} are given by

ℒ⊃\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\supset −cosθRcosθϕyϕ​χ​ν(ϕχ¯LνR)+h.c.\displaystyle-\cos\theta_{R}\cos\theta_{\phi}y_{\phi\chi\nu}(\phi\bar{\chi}_{L}\nu_{R})+h.c.
−sinθRcosθϕyϕ​χ​ν(ϕχ¯LχR)+h.c.\displaystyle-\sin\theta_{R}\cos\theta_{\phi}y_{\phi\chi\nu}(\phi\bar{\chi}_{L}\chi_{R})+h.c. (11)

The vertex factors contributing to the dark matter absorption process in fig. 1 can then be written explicitly:

Ye​e\displaystyle Y_{ee} =mevsinθϕ,\displaystyle=\frac{m_{e}}{v}\sin\theta_{\phi}\,, (12)
Yχ​ν\displaystyle Y_{\chi\nu} =yϕ​χ​νcosθRcosθϕ.\displaystyle=y_{\phi\chi\nu}\cos\theta_{R}\cos\theta_{\phi}\,. (13)

See appendix A for the full expressions, including additional couplings proportional to neutrino mass.

III Phenomenology

III.1 Direct Detection

In a direct detection experiment, the absorption of χ\chi can transfer sufficient energy to ionise an atomic electron. This signal can be detected in large volume argon and xenon time projection chambers via subsequent scintillation and secondary ionisation. The differential rate for dark matter absorption via the operator (χ¯​PR​ν)​(e¯​e)/Λ2(\bar{\chi}P_{R}\nu)(\bar{e}e)/\Lambda^{2} was calculated in Refs. [8, 9] for a xenon target. The event rate is proportional to the effective absorption cross-section,

σe≡mχ24​π​Λ4.\sigma_{e}\equiv\frac{m_{\chi}^{2}}{4\pi\Lambda^{4}}\,. (14)

The projected sensitivities of current and proposed future xenon experiments to σe\sigma_{e} were calculated by Ref. [8]. The authors assumed a detection efficiency equal to that of the XENON1T experiment [12], with an energy threshold of 1 keV (sensitive to absorption events for mχ≳3m_{\chi}\gtrsim 3 keV), and determined the projected sensitivity by requiring at least 10 events during an experiment’s full exposure. Here, we predominantly focus on the sensitivity at the proposed XLZD detector [13] (assuming an exposure of 200 tonne-years), which offers the best prospects in the foreseeable future.

The typical momentum transfer in the absorption process is of order mχm_{\chi}. The EFT description is therefore valid provided mϕ≫mχm_{\phi}\gg m_{\chi}. In terms of the parameters of our model, the effective absorption cross-section in this limit is

σe\displaystyle\sigma_{e} =mχ2​Ye​e2​Yχ​ν24​π​mϕ4\displaystyle=\frac{m_{\chi}^{2}Y_{ee}^{2}Y_{\chi\nu}^{2}}{4\pi m_{\phi}^{4}} (15)
=sin2⁡θϕ​cos2⁡θϕ​cos2⁡θR​(mev)2​yϕ​χ​ν24​π​mχ2mϕ4.\displaystyle=\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}\cos^{2}\theta_{\phi}\cos^{2}\theta_{R}\left(\frac{m_{e}}{v}\right)^{2}\frac{y_{\phi\chi\nu}^{2}}{4\pi}\frac{m_{\chi}^{2}}{m_{\phi}^{4}}\,. (16)

To assess the potential sensitivity of direct detection to our model, we compare this expression with the projections of Ref. [8]. This is justified only within the regime of validity of the EFT, with corrections of order (mχ/mϕ)2(m_{\chi}/m_{\phi})^{2} as mϕm_{\phi} approaches mχm_{\chi}.

It is evident from eq. 16 that the most interesting parameter space for direct detection is where the mixing is small between χR′\chi_{R}^{\prime} and νR′\nu_{R}^{\prime} (cos⁡θR≃1\cos\theta_{R}\simeq 1) and where the Yukawa coupling in the dark sector is large (yϕ​χ​ν≃1y_{\phi\chi\nu}\simeq 1). This region of parameter space corresponds to ⟨ϕ′⟩+Mχ​ν≪mχ\left<\phi^{\prime}\right>+M_{\chi\nu}\ll m_{\chi}. In subsequent sections we always take cos⁡θR=1\cos\theta_{R}=1.

III.2 Dark Matter Decay

The dark matter is unstable and can decay into final states featuring neutrinos and photons. There must be an odd number of neutrinos in the final state, since χ\chi is fermionic. Given the suppression of the decay χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma, the dominant decay modes are χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma, and the invisible mode χ→ν​ν​ν\chi\to\nu\nu\nu.

As discussed in section II, the softly broken ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry naturally suppresses the otherwise leading visible decay mode χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma. In the massless neutrino limit, when yH​νy_{H\nu} and hence sin⁡θL\sin\theta_{L} vanish, the only coupling of χ\chi to the SM is through the scalar portal, and the visible decay modes must proceed via the ϕ−H\phi-H mixing. The χ→ν​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma decay vanishes in this limit, meaning that the dominant visible decay mode is χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma, which occurs at one-loop via the diagrams shown in fig. 2. The corresponding decay width is

Γχ→ν​γ​γ=Yχ​ν2​sin2⁡θϕ2048​π5​mχ3​α2v2​Iv​i​s​(mϕ,mχ),\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma}=\frac{Y_{\chi\nu}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}}{2048\pi^{5}m_{\chi}^{3}}\frac{\alpha^{2}}{v^{2}}I_{vis}(m_{\phi},m_{\chi})\,, (17)

with

Iv​i​s​(mϕ,mχ)=(116)2​∫0mχ2d​s12​(mχ2−s12mϕ2−s12)2​s122.I_{vis}(m_{\phi},m_{\chi})=\left(\frac{11}{6}\right)^{2}\int_{0}^{m_{\chi}^{2}}\text{d}s_{12}\left(\frac{m_{\chi}^{2}-s_{12}}{m_{\phi}^{2}-s_{12}}\right)^{2}s_{12}^{2}\,. (18)

The factor of (11/6)2(11/6)^{2} comes from the loop function in the limit where mχm_{\chi} is much smaller than the SM fermion and WW boson masses. In the regime where mϕ≫mχm_{\phi}\gg m_{\chi}, the width can be written purely in terms of the dark matter mass and effective absorption cross-section44 4 This result differs by a factor of (11/4)2(11/4)^{2} from the EFT result in Ref. [9], since in that case only electrons run in the loop.:

Γχ→ν​γ​γ≃1.8×10−27​sec−1​(mχ10​ keV)5​(σe10−50​ cm2).\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma}\simeq 1.8\times 10^{-27}\text{sec}^{-1}\left(\frac{m_{\chi}}{10\text{ keV}}\right)^{5}\left(\frac{\sigma_{e}}{10^{-50}\text{ cm}^{2}}\right)\,. (19)

This provides a good approximation to eq. 17, up to an 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) factor, even when mϕ∼mχm_{\phi}\sim m_{\chi}. This decay rate must be less than the upper bound imposed by diffuse X-ray measurements [14].

Figure 3 shows the X-ray limits on χ→ν​γ​γ\chi\to\nu\gamma\gamma decays in terms of the dark matter absorption effective cross-section as a function of mχm_{\chi}. The sharp changes in the excluded region (shaded blue) near mχ=10, 40m_{\chi}=10,\,40\,keV arise from the differing sensitivities of the X-ray telescopes used to set the bound. Also shown in the figure is the projected direct detection sensitivity of LZ (assuming 15.3 tonne-years exposure) and the proposed next generation experiment XLZD (assuming 200 tonne-years exposure) from Ref. [8]. We will subsequently focus on the sensitivity of XLZD as it offers the best prospects in the foreseeable future. We find that, given the X-ray bounds, XLZD will only provide new sensitivity for dark matter masses mχ≲15m_{\chi}\lesssim 15 keV. In subsequent sections, we analyse a benchmark dark matter mass of mχ=10m_{\chi}=10 keV.

We now turn to the invisible decay, χ→ν​ν​ν\chi\to\nu\nu\nu. This decay can occur at tree level when neutrinos are massive, as can be seen from fig. 1 by replacing the electrons with neutrinos and employing crossing symmetry. The tree-level diagram vanishes in the massless neutrino limit, as do one-loop diagrams featuring νL\nu_{L} in the final state. However, the invisible decay into three νR\nu_{R} can still occur at one-loop via the ϕ3\phi^{3} coupling, as shown in fig. 4.

The decay width of χ→ν​ν​ν\chi\to\nu\nu\nu is given by

This differs from eq. 20 only by an 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) factor, even when mϕ∼mχm_{\phi}\sim m_{\chi}. For successful structure formation, (Γχ→ν​ν​ν)−1(\Gamma_{\chi\to\nu\nu\nu})^{-1} must be greater than 468 Gyr [16]. This places an upper bound on the ϕ3\phi^{3} coupling of K≲10−11​mϕK\lesssim 10^{-11}m_{\phi}. Neglecting possible cancellations between the terms in KK, this translates into strong upper bounds on the scalar parameters:

|κ3|≲10−6​ eV​(mϕ200​ keV),\displaystyle|\kappa_{3}|\lesssim 10^{-6}\text{ eV}\left(\frac{m_{\phi}}{200\text{ keV}}\right)\,, (24)
|κ4​⟨ϕ′⟩|≲10−6​ eV​(mϕ200​ keV),\displaystyle|\kappa_{4}\left<\phi^{\prime}\right>|\lesssim 10^{-6}\text{ eV}\left(\frac{m_{\phi}}{200\text{ keV}}\right)\,, (25)
|δ2|≲3×10−11​(10−7sin⁡θϕ)​(mϕ200​ keV).\displaystyle|\delta_{2}|\lesssim 3\times 10^{-11}\left(\frac{10^{-7}}{\sin\theta_{\phi}}\right)\left(\frac{m_{\phi}}{200\text{ keV}}\right). (26)

Simultaneously satisfying these bounds and obtaining a value of sin⁡θϕ\sin\theta_{\phi} that is large enough to be of phenomenological interest likely requires values of the scalar potential parameters that are unstable under radiative corrections. Naturalness aside, the above bounds do not restrict the prospects for direct detection. The scalar parameters relevant for direct detection are mϕm_{\phi}, sin2⁡θϕ\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}, and ⟨ϕ′⟩\left<\phi^{\prime}\right> (which leads to χR−νR\chi_{R}-\nu_{R} mixing). The first two of these are unconstrained by the invisible decay bound. Specifically, mϕ2∼κ2m_{\phi}^{2}\sim\kappa_{2} and sin2⁡θϕ∼δ12/mh2\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}\sim\delta_{1}^{2}/m_{h}^{2} when eqs. 24, 25 and 26 are satisfied. Furthermore, the bound on |κ4​⟨ϕ′⟩||\kappa_{4}\left<\phi^{\prime}\right>| imposed by eq. 25 is consistent with the limit ⟨ϕ′⟩≪mχ\left<\phi^{\prime}\right>\ll m_{\chi} in which the direct detection prospects are maximised (i.e. yϕ​χ​ν≃1y_{\phi\chi\nu}\simeq 1 and cos⁡θR≃1\cos\theta_{R}\simeq 1).

III.3 Mediator Constraints

There are also strong constraints on the scalar mediator ϕ\phi which, as we shall show, further restrict the parameter space that could be probed through direct detection. The most relevant constraints come from astrophysics. Production of ϕ\phi can occur in stars and the core of supernovae, leading to energy loss as ϕ\phi or its decay products, χ\chi and νR\nu_{R}, escape the stellar medium. We utilise the limits derived in Refs. [17, 18]. Due to the fast decay of ϕ→χ​νR\phi\to\chi\nu_{R} in our model, trapping of ϕ\phi within a stellar or supernova core does not occur, however the decay products χ\chi and νR\nu_{R} can be trapped due to the process χ​N↔νR​N\chi N\leftrightarrow\nu_{R}N, depending on the value of yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu}. We calculate the thermally averaged mean free path for this process using the same stellar/supernova parameters as Refs. [17, 18].

Figure 5 shows the bounds from stellar and SN1987A luminosity on the mϕ−sin2⁡θϕm_{\phi}-\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi} parameter space. The upper edges of these regions correspond to where the mean free path of χ\chi or νR\nu_{R} is less than 10% of the stellar or supernova core radius. This depends on yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} and we show results for yϕ​χ​ν=1y_{\phi\chi\nu}=1 and yϕ​χ​ν=10−2y_{\phi\chi\nu}=10^{-2}. Note that obtaining a precise bound in the trapping regime would require a more detailed treatment. Also shown in fig. 5 are constraints on the scalar mediator from searches for invisible meson decays. The fixed target experiment NA62 constrains the kaon decay K→π​ϕK\to\pi\phi [19], while BaBar constrains B→K​ϕB\to K\phi [20]. BaBar provides the strongest constraint in the mϕ≃300m_{\phi}\simeq 300 MeV – 1 GeV region, where the supernova core is not hot enough to produce ϕ\phi. The region where mϕ<mχm_{\phi}<m_{\chi} is excluded by dark matter stability, since here the decay channel χ→ϕ​ν\chi\to\phi\nu is available.

For yϕ​χ​ν≲0.1y_{\phi\chi\nu}\lesssim 0.1, the combination of SN1987A and NA62 excludes sin2⁡θϕ≳10−14\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}\gtrsim 10^{-14} for mϕ≲300m_{\phi}\lesssim 300 MeV, with horizontal branch stars providing stronger limits for mϕ≲70m_{\phi}\lesssim 70 keV. If yϕ​χ​ν≳0.1y_{\phi\chi\nu}\gtrsim 0.1, there may be unconstrained windows of parameter space between the NA62 and stellar/SN limits.

Overlaid on fig. 5 is the projected sensitivity of XLZD to mχ=10m_{\chi}=10 keV for a range of yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} couplings. We see that much of the parameter space accessible to direct detection has already been probed by searches for the mediator. New regions of parameter space are accessible by XLZD, provided yϕ​χ​ν≳10−2y_{\phi\chi\nu}\gtrsim 10^{-2}. These results are qualitatively the same across the relevant mass range, 4 keV ≲mχ≲15\lesssim m_{\chi}\lesssim 15 keV. As mentioned, corrections of order (mχ/mϕ)2(m_{\chi}/m_{\phi})^{2} apply to the projected XLZD sensitivities as mϕm_{\phi} approaches mχm_{\chi} and the EFT begins to break down.

IV Dark Matter Production

We now turn to the production of dark matter in the early universe. To avoid conflicting with bounds on the effective number of relativistic degrees of freedom during BBN and at the time of the CMB [21], we require that the dark sector never enters into equilibrium with the SM bath. On the other hand, χ\chi, ϕ\phi, and νR\nu_{R} may achieve thermal equilibrium amongst themselves. This is expected to be the case in the regions of parameter space of interest for direct detection, where the Yukawa coupling in the dark sector is relatively large, yϕ​χ​ν≳10−2y_{\phi\chi\nu}\gtrsim 10^{-2} (see fig. 5). Given some initial population, for example produced via freeze-in, the dark sector reaches equilibrium and subsequent freeze-out in the dark sector sets the final dark matter relic abundance.55 5 The relic abundance can be produced purely by freeze-in from the SM sector in the parameter space where yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} is highly suppressed. However, this would not yield a direct detection signal. This process of freeze-in, thermalisation and freeze-out in the dark sector was first explored in the context of a dark photon mediator in Ref. [22] and more recently in a scalar portal model in Ref. [23]. In the following two sections we discuss in turn thermalisation and freeze-out in detail.

IV.1 Freeze-in and Thermalisation

The dark sector will be populated through freeze-in from the SM thermal bath, via processes such as f​f¯→χ​ν¯Rf\bar{f}\to\chi\bar{\nu}_{R}, where ff denotes SM fermions. This freeze-in production will continue until the SM bath temperature, TS​MT_{SM}, falls below the electron mass and the process e+​e−→χ​ν¯Re^{+}e^{-}\to\chi\bar{\nu}_{R} ceases to be efficient. In addition to this irreducible contribution, there may be additional processes that populate the dark sector, for example inflaton decay during reheating.

For the larger values of the scalar mixing that we consider, sin2⁡θϕ≳10−14\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}\gtrsim 10^{-14}, the reheat temperature should be well below the electroweak scale. This is because for higher reheat temperatures, electroweak processes, such as W​Z→W​ϕWZ\to W\phi, can cause the dark sector to enter equilibrium with the SM bath. We use micrOMEGAS-v5.3 [24] to numerically calculate the irreducible population of dark sector particles created from (tree-level) freeze-in processes, and estimate that for sin2⁡θϕ=10−14\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}=10^{-14}, a reheat temperature of TR≲20T_{R}\lesssim 20 GeV is required. For smaller values of sin2⁡θϕ\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}, the reheat temperature can be higher, and for sin2⁡θϕ≲10−16\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}\lesssim 10^{-16} the dark sector remains out of equilibrium with the SM regardless of the reheat temperature.

As the dark sector is populated, ϕ,χ\phi,\chi and νR\nu_{R} interact through the yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} coupling, which can lead to their thermalisation. Determining whether the dark sector reaches internal equilibrium, and the value of the dark sector temperature TDT_{D}, requires solving the Boltzmann equations for the momentum distributions generated by freeze-in. However, thermalisation is expected to occur rapidly in the parameter space of interest for direct detection due to the large values of the coupling (10−2≲yϕ​χ​ν≲110^{-2}\lesssim y_{\phi\chi\nu}\lesssim 1). Hence, in the following we simply assume that equilibrium is achieved and consider the temperature in the dark sector as a free parameter. To support this assumption, in appendix B we compare the dark sector interaction rates to the expansion rate and show that for the relevant range of dark sector temperatures and couplings, kinetic and chemical equilibrium are maintained until TS​M∼me/3T_{SM}\sim m_{e}/3 and all freeze-in processes have effectively ceased.

The thermalised dark sector particles contribute to the effective number of relativistic degrees of freedom by an amount that depends on the temperature ratio TD/TS​MT_{D}/T_{SM}. The limits on Δ​Ne​f​f\Delta N_{eff} from both BBN and CMB [25] translate to an upper bound on the dark sector temperature of TD≲0.4×TS​MT_{D}\lesssim 0.4\times T_{SM}.

IV.2 Freeze-out of Dark Matter

Next, we calculate the relic abundance of dark matter produced via freeze-out within the dark sector. The equilibrium number density of χ\chi at a dark sector temperature TDT_{D} is given by

nχe​q​(TD)=gχ​mχ2​TD2​π2​K2​(mχ/TD),n_{\chi}^{eq}\left(T_{D}\right)=\frac{g_{\chi}m_{\chi}^{2}T_{D}}{2\pi^{2}}K_{2}\left(m_{\chi}/T_{D}\right)\,, (27)

where gχ=4g_{\chi}=4 and K2K_{2} is a modified Bessel function of the second kind. We divide the number density by the SM entropy density to obtain the yield, or comoving number density66 6 After the freeze-in processes have ended, the entropy density of the SM and dark sectors are (approximately) separately conserved.:

Yχe​q​(TD,TS​M)≡nχe​q​(TD)s⁡(TS​M).Y^{eq}_{\chi}\left(T_{D},T_{SM}\right)\equiv\frac{n^{eq}_{\chi}(T_{D})}{s(T_{SM})}\,. (28)

Figure 6 shows the equilibrium yield of χ\chi for various ratios of TD/TS​MT_{D}/T_{SM} as a function of TS​MT_{SM}. The observed present day yield of χ\chi, shown as a horizontal purple dashed line, must be obtained via freeze-out from these equilibrium curves. Hence, to achieve the correct relic abundance requires 0.08≲TD/TS​M≲0.40.08\lesssim T_{D}/T_{SM}\lesssim 0.4 at the onset of freeze-out, with the upper limit coming from the bound on Δ​Ne​f​f\Delta N_{eff}.

We now solve the Boltzmann equation across the viable range of TD/TS​MT_{D}/T_{SM}, to find the range of yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} that gives the observed present day dark matter abundance. The Boltzmann equation for the dark matter number density, nχ​(t)n_{\chi}(t), is

n˙χ+3​H​nχ=−⟨σ​v⟩TD​(nχ2−(nχe​q)2),\dot{n}_{\chi}+3Hn_{\chi}=-\left<\sigma v\right>_{T_{D}}\left(n_{\chi}^{2}-(n_{\chi}^{eq})^{2}\right)\,, (29)

where ⟨σ​v⟩TD\left<\sigma v\right>_{T_{D}} is the thermally averaged cross-section times velocity evaluated at temperature TD​(t)T_{D}(t), and we have assumed Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics. At the time of freeze-out, the relevant number-changing processes are χ​χ→νR​νR\chi\chi\to\nu_{R}\nu_{R}, χ¯​χ¯→ν¯R​ν¯R\bar{\chi}\bar{\chi}\to\bar{\nu}_{R}\bar{\nu}_{R}, and χ​χ¯→νR​ν¯R\chi\bar{\chi}\to\nu_{R}\bar{\nu}_{R}. We use micrOMEGAS-v5.3 [24] to numerically calculate ⟨σ​v⟩\left<\sigma v\right> as a function of temperature. When the Δ​Ne​f​f\Delta N_{eff} bound is satisfied, the Hubble parameter H⁡(t)H(t) is largely determined by the SM degrees of freedom. In addition, the effective number of entropic degrees of freedom is approximately constant during freeze-out, d​g∗S/d​TS​M≃0\mathrm{d}g_{*S}/\mathrm{d}T_{SM}\simeq 0. Hence, expressed in terms of the yield, Yχ≡nχ/s⁡(TS​M)Y_{\chi}\equiv n_{\chi}/s(T_{SM}), the Boltzmann equation becomes

d​Yχd​TS​M=s⁡(TS​M)H⁡(TS​M)​TS​M​⟨σ​v⟩TD​(Yχ2−(Yχe​q)2).\frac{dY_{\chi}}{dT_{SM}}=\frac{s(T_{SM})}{H(T_{SM})T_{SM}}\left<\sigma v\right>_{T_{D}}\left(Y_{\chi}^{2}-\left(Y_{\chi}^{eq}\right)^{2}\right)\,. (30)

Figure 7 shows the freeze out of χ\chi within the dark sector at the extremal allowed values of TDT_{D}. The red curve shows the hottest dark sector, TD=0.4×TS​MT_{D}=0.4\times T_{SM}, while the blue curve shows the coldest dark sector, TD=0.08×TS​MT_{D}=0.08\times T_{SM}. In each case the Yukawa coupling yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} has been chosen to obtain the observed dark matter abundance. For the hotter dark sector, yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} must be larger so that equilibrium is prolonged and there is sufficient annihilation of dark matter into neutrinos. The solutions reveal that for χ\chi to account for the present day yield, yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} must be in the range 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} to 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} for mϕ=200m_{\phi}=200 keV. This range varies linearly with mϕm_{\phi}, since ⟨σ​v⟩∝(yϕ​χ​ν/mϕ)4\left<\sigma v\right>\propto\left(y_{\phi\chi\nu}/m_{\phi}\right)^{4}. Furthermore, the required yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} varies negligibly across the range of mχm_{\chi} of interest for direct detection (4 keV ≲mχ≲15\lesssim m_{\chi}\lesssim 15 keV). Note that the results are independent of sin2⁡θϕ\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi}, since all interactions with the SM during freeze-out are Boltzmann suppressed.

Finally, we consider the potential of direct detection to probe the values of yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} that yield the correct dark matter abundance. From fig. 5, we see that for mϕ=200m_{\phi}=200 keV and 2×10−4<yϕ​χ​ν<5×10−42\times 10^{-4}<y_{\phi\chi\nu}<5\times 10^{-4}, the sensitivity of XLZD to sin2⁡θϕ\sin^{2}\theta_{\phi} lies well within the parameter space already excluded by SN1987A. Furthermore, given that the relevant range of yϕ​χ​νy_{\phi\chi\nu} depends linearly on mϕm_{\phi}, as discussed above, this conclusion holds for the full range of mϕm_{\phi} in fig. 5. Hence, after imposing the correct relic abundance, there is no unconstrained parameter space that can be probed via dark matter absorption at XLZD.

V Conclusion

Fermionic dark matter absorption is an interesting direct detection signal that has recently been studied using effective field theory. Motivated by this, we have constructed a UV complete model of the scalar operator associated with this signature. Our model can achieve the correct cosmological relic abundance via freeze-out within the dark sector. We find that visible dark matter decays, in conjunction with stellar and supernova constraints on the scalar mediator, provide strong constraints. The parameter space that is consistent with these bounds and could also be probed at a next-generation direct detection experiment such as XLZD under-predicts the relic density. This case study demonstrates that the absorption signal cannot be observed in upcoming direct detection experiments for a minimal, realistic model of scalar-mediated dark matter. It would therefore be interesting to construct other, non-minimal models which have this signal as well as a consistent cosmological history yielding the correct relic abundance.

Appendix B Dark Sector Equilibrium

If the dark sector remains in chemical and kinetic equilibrium after all freeze-in processes have effectively ceased, the freeze-in and freeze-out eras of dark matter production can be treated separately, as in section IV. In this appendix, we show that chemical and kinetic equilibrium are indeed maintained post-freeze-in for the range of dark sector temperatures and couplings that allow for the freeze-out of χ\chi with the correct relic abundance.

Chemical equilibrium is maintained between χ\chi and νR\nu_{R} when the annihilation rate of dark matter to sterile neutrinos is greater than the Hubble parameter. We calculate the ratio of these two quantities as a function of TDT_{D} and TS​MT_{SM}:

ΓannH=nχe​q​(TD)​⟨σ​v⟩TDH⁡(TS​M),\frac{\Gamma_{\mathrm{ann}}}{H}=\frac{n_{\chi}^{eq}(T_{D})\left<\sigma v\right>_{T_{D}}}{H(T_{SM})}\,, (62)

where nχe​q​(TD)n_{\chi}^{eq}(T_{D}) is the equilibrium number density of χ\chi and ⟨σ​v⟩TD\left<\sigma v\right>_{T_{D}} is the thermally averaged dark matter annihilation cross-section times velocity at temperature TDT_{D}. As in section IV, we use micrOMEGAS-v5.3 [24] to numerically calculate ⟨σ​v⟩\left<\sigma v\right>, including contributions from χ​χ→νR​νR\chi\chi\to\nu_{R}\nu_{R}, χ¯​χ¯→ν¯R​ν¯R\bar{\chi}\bar{\chi}\to\bar{\nu}_{R}\bar{\nu}_{R}, and χ​χ¯→νR​ν¯R\chi\bar{\chi}\to\nu_{R}\bar{\nu}_{R}. We work in the limit of massless neutrinos and take cos⁡θR=1\cos\theta_{R}=1. The Δ​Ne​f​f\Delta N_{eff} bound discussed in section IV enforces TD<0.4×TS​MT_{D}<0.4\times T_{SM}, such that the Hubble rate is largely determined by the SM degrees of freedom. Kinetic equilibrium is maintained whenever chemical equilibrium holds and persists to lower temperatures, since the annihilation rate is suppressed by a factor of nχe​qn_{\chi}^{eq} compared with the scattering rate χ​νR↔χ​νR\chi\nu_{R}\leftrightarrow\chi\nu_{R}.

Figure 8 shows Γann/H\Gamma_{\mathrm{ann}}/H as a function of TS​MT_{SM} for two dark sector couplings, yϕ​χ​ν=10−2y_{\phi\chi\nu}=10^{-2} and 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, and two dark sector temperatures, TD/TS​M=0.4T_{D}/T_{SM}=0.4 and 0.08. These temperatures correspond to the upper and lower bounds discussed in section IV.2, between which successful freeze-out of χ\chi with the correct relic abundance can occur. At SM bath temperatures below TS​M∼me/3T_{SM}\sim m_{e}/3, shown as a vertical grey dashed line, freeze-in processes from the SM bath are Boltzmann suppressed. We see that for 0.08≲TD/TS​M≲0.40.08\lesssim T_{D}/T_{SM}\lesssim 0.4, dark sector equilibrium is maintained both during and beyond the end of the freeze-in era, provided yϕ​χ​ν≳2×10−4y_{\phi\chi\nu}\gtrsim 2\times 10^{-4}. This supports the assumption made in section IV that the dark sector enters equilibrium as ϕ\phi, χ\chi and νR\nu_{R} are produced via portal interactions, and that the freeze-in and freeze-out eras of dark matter production can be treated separately.
